title: Cliff Click @ VMSS16: Bits of Advice For the VM Writer
summary: Cliff Click, author of HotSpot's JIT compiler, shares hard-won advice for people writing virtual machines at the VMSS16 workshop. Topics include interpreters, JITs and performance lessons.
why_hn: HN recommends it, and Cliff Click's talks in general, as practical wisdom from someone who built HotSpot and worked on Azul's VMs.

title: But why would light "slow down"? | Visualizing Feynman's lecture on the refractive index
summary: 3Blue1Brown visualizes Feynman's lecture on the refractive index, explaining why light appears to slow down in glass and why the effect depends on color. It builds the idea from waves produced by oscillating charges in the material.
why_hn: HN considers it among the clearest accessible explanations of what refractive index actually is and how light moves through transparent matter.

title: Keep your goals to yourself | Derek Sivers
summary: A four-minute TED talk in which Derek Sivers argues that announcing your goals can make you less likely to achieve them. He cites psychology research going back to the 1920s.
why_hn: Commenters credit it with changing how they handle plans and recommend it as a short, sourced talk.

title: Why I, as a black man, attend KKK rallies. | Daryl Davis | TEDxNaperville
summary: Black musician Daryl Davis tells how a chance encounter led him to befriend Ku Klux Klan members and seek the source of racial hate. He argues that sitting down and talking with people can change them.
why_hn: Recommended in moderation and deplatforming debates as a case for engagement and compassion over exclusion.

title: Parking Laws Are Strangling America | Climate Town
summary: Climate Town traces the history of American parking minimums, how they came from shaky research and ITE guides, and how they shape zoning, cities and housing costs. It is a long, comedic video essay.
why_hn: Recommended as a fun but well-researched explanation of why parking requirements are arbitrary and harmful.

title: Our democracy no longer represents the people. Here's how we fix it | Larry Lessig | TEDxMidAtlantic
summary: Harvard law professor Lawrence Lessig argues that US democracy is corrupted by money, since a tiny fraction of the population effectively funds who gets elected. He says fixing this must come before addressing issues like climate change or student debt.
why_hn: It is HN's go-to link in threads on lobbying, campaign finance and political dysfunction, as a clear statement of Lessig's root-cause argument.

title: DAIRY IS SCARY!
summary: Vegan advocate Erin Janus explains the dairy industry in about five minutes, covering how milk is produced and the treatment of cows and calves. It is an advocacy piece and includes graphic material.
why_hn: HN commenters in veganism and food threads link it as a short, info-dense explanation that some say opened their eyes, though others dispute it.

title: Jordan Peterson debate on the gender pay gap, campus protests and postmodernism
summary: Channel 4 News's full interview with Jordan Peterson, in which Cathy Newman presses him on the gender pay gap, patriarchy, campus protests and postmodernism. It was widely discussed for its confrontational style.
why_hn: HN cites it as the classic example of an interviewer misrepresenting a guest, though opinions on who came out better differ.

title: Inside the Mind of a Master Procrastinator | Tim Urban | TED
summary: Tim Urban's TED talk on why people procrastinate, covering YouTube binges and Wikipedia rabbit holes. It ends with the life-calendar idea as a nudge to act before time runs out.
why_hn: Recommended as a funny, empathetic take on procrastination and the origin of the life calendar concept.

title: Fat Chance: Fructose 2.0
summary: Robert Lustig of UCSF updates his sugar talk, arguing that fructose and processed foods drive obesity and metabolic syndrome through their endocrine effects. It is a roughly 90-minute university lecture.
why_hn: Recommended as a follow-up to Lustig's original sugar talk for the metabolic details of fructose.

title: How to learn any language in six months | Chris Lonsdale | TEDxLingnanUniversity
summary: Chris Lonsdale presents a TEDx talk on how adults can learn a language in about six months, centering on immersion, comprehensible input and a practical learning methodology.
why_hn: HN recommends it as an efficient, practical approach to adult language learning, with one commenter saying it changed their life.

title: Energy Investments Dialogue | Bill Gates | Global Energy Forum
summary: Bill Gates at Stanford's Global Energy Forum argues that cheaper solar, wind and storage are not nearly enough to stop climate change. He discusses natural gas, a carbon tax, nuclear, battery costs and the responsibilities of developing versus developed economies.
why_hn: Cited in energy threads for Gates's argument on why batteries and renewables alone fall short and nuclear is needed.

title: How Far Are The Nearest Stars?
summary: Cody's Lab builds a 200-billionth-scale model to show how far away the nearest stars are, using parallax and light speed. A short astronomy explainer on interstellar distances.
why_hn: Recommended whenever threads need an intuition for the vast distances between stars.

title: NSA operation ORCHESTRA: Annual Status Report
summary: Poul-Henning Kamp's FOSDEM 2014 talk is a hypothetical account of how an intelligence agency such as the NSA would sabotage open source software, standards and online discussion. It covers Skype's history, OpenSSL and psyops against standards.
why_hn: HN returned to it repeatedly, especially after Heartbleed, as an eye-opening argument about subverting open source and standards.

title: Simon Sinek on Millennials in the Workplace
summary: An excerpt of Simon Sinek on Inside Quest discussing millennials in the workplace. He covers parenting, technology, social media dopamine and what that means for managers.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it for its take on managing young employees and on how technology and approval-seeking affect behavior.

title: Jeff Bezos - Regret Minimization Framework
summary: A three-minute clip of Jeff Bezos describing his Regret Minimization Framework: imagining yourself at 80 to decide whether to leave a Wall Street job to start Amazon.
why_hn: HN commenters cite it whenever someone asks whether to quit a job or start a company, as a simple decision heuristic.

title: Why You Should Put YOUR MASK On First (My Brain Without Oxygen) - Smarter Every Day 157
summary: Destin Sandlin of Smarter Every Day undergoes hypoxia training and experiences his own impaired thinking as oxygen is withdrawn. The video shows how quickly and unnoticeably oxygen deprivation degrades judgment, illustrating why you put your own mask on first.
why_hn: It is the go-to demonstration of how hypoxia silently disables decision making, cited in threads on altitude, flying, diving, CO2 and breathwork.

title: Classic Game Postmortem: Ultima Online
summary: A 2018 GDC panel where Raph Koster, Starr Long, Richard Garriott and Rich Vogel look back on what went right and wrong building and running Ultima Online. They share candid stories from the early days, including player behavior and server architecture.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a transparent MMO postmortem and as the source of the story that the term 'shard' originated with Ultima Online.

title: Cheng Lou - On the Spectrum of Abstraction at react-europe 2016
summary: Cheng Lou's react-europe 2016 talk lays out a mental framework for thinking about abstraction levels in JavaScript tooling, from Angular and Grunt to Webpack and React. It uses that framework to reason about the cost of abstractions and how to choose between competing solutions.
why_hn: HN points to it as thought-provoking material on the tradeoffs and costs of abstraction, especially in frontend tooling debates.

title: The Pervert's Guide to Computer Programming Languages - SXSW
summary: A SXSW talk by W Watson that uses Lacanian psychoanalysis, with nods to Zizek, to critique popular programming languages. It argues that people choose and defend languages for emotional and ideological reasons rather than rational ones.
why_hn: HN recommends it as an entertaining and eye-opening look at the irrational psychology behind language preferences, though some note it is not scientifically precise.

title: Hacker Way: Rethinking Web App Development at Facebook
summary: Facebook engineers explain why they abandoned the traditional MVC paradigm for a more functional architecture, introducing Flux and React. They use the unread-message-count bug as a case study of the problems of bidirectional data flow at scale.
why_hn: HN points to it as the original talk that explains the motivation behind React, Flux and Redux, and that sold some commenters on React.

title: This equation will change how you see the world (the logistic map)
summary: A Veritasium video on the logistic map, showing how a simple population equation leads to chaos and bifurcation. It connects the idea to convection, neuron firing and the Mandelbrot set, with interactive animations.
why_hn: HN commenters call it a favourite Veritasium video, praised for how a simple equation reveals surprisingly complex patterns.

title: KGB Defector Yuri Bezmenov 1985 Interview. Explains KGB Manipulation of US Public Opinion
summary: A 1985 interview by G. Edward Griffin with former KGB operative Yuri Bezmenov. He describes long-running Soviet efforts at ideological subversion and manipulation of US public opinion.
why_hn: HN commenters bring it up in threads on propaganda, influence operations and platforms like TikTok, saying it feels more relevant than ever.

title: Sparks of AGI: early experiments with GPT-4
summary: Sebastien Bubeck presents the Sparks of AGI paper at MIT, showing early experiments with GPT-4 across many domains and asking whether artificial intelligence has arrived. It includes the TikZ unicorn example.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a thought-provoking talk from a researcher with early GPT-4 access, especially for the unicorn degrading under safety tuning.

title: How Great Leaders Inspire Action | Simon Sinek | TED
summary: Simon Sinek's TED talk presents the 'golden circle' model: great leaders and companies inspire action by starting with why they do something, before how or what. He illustrates it with Apple, Martin Luther King, the Wright brothers and, as a counterexample, TiVo.
why_hn: HN commenters cite it to explain why customers buy into a company's beliefs rather than its specs, especially in threads about Apple, marketing and product messaging.

title: OK Go - This Too Shall Pass - Rube Goldberg Machine - Official Video
summary: OK Go's music video for This Too Shall Pass, featuring a huge Rube Goldberg machine built in a warehouse in Los Angeles with Syyn Labs. The band interacts with the contraption in one continuous take.
why_hn: HN points to it as an example of ambitious, practical-effects creativity in music videos, made without CGI.

title: The Boeing 787: Broken Dreams l Al Jazeera Investigations
summary: An Al Jazeera investigation into Boeing's 787 Dreamliner, featuring current and former engineers who voice safety concerns. It covers quality control problems at the South Carolina plant and the roots of the battery problems that grounded the plane.
why_hn: Boeing threads cite it as early evidence of deep cultural and quality problems at Boeing, years before the 737 MAX crashes.

title: A Selfish Argument for Making the World a Better Place – Egoistic Altruism
summary: Kurzgesagt makes a selfish case for improving the world, arguing that helping people far away raises prosperity and innovation for everyone, including yourself. The animated video frames this as egoistic altruism and positive-sum cooperation.
why_hn: HN commenters link it to argue for cooperation and engagement over isolation, and as an accessible statement of positive-sum thinking.

title: Richard Feynman on Pseudoscience
summary: A two-minute clip of Richard Feynman explaining why he considers much of social science pseudoscience. He stresses how easy it is to fool yourself and how much care real knowledge takes.
why_hn: Commenters post it whenever a thread touches on soft sciences, replication problems, or what counts as real science.

title: Avie Tevanian: CMU math whiz goes from Mach to NeXT to Apple Software Chief | Oral History Part 1
summary: A Computer History Museum oral history with Avie Tevanian covering his math talent, work on the Mach microkernel at CMU, joining NeXT, leading NEXTSTEP development and the 1996 Apple acquisition.
why_hn: Recommended as a long, rich first-hand account of Mach, NeXT and Apple history and of working for Steve Jobs.

title: The Neuroscience of Consciousness – with Anil Seth
summary: Neuroscientist Anil Seth gives a Royal Institution lecture on the science of consciousness. He separates conscious level, content and self, and argues that experience arises from the brain's predictive inference.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as a clear, in-depth lecture on consciousness as a process of prediction.

title: FULL INTERVIEW with Yuri Bezmenov: The Four Stages of Ideological Subversion (1984)
summary: The full 1984 interview with Yuri Bezmenov, a former KGB operative, in which he lays out four stages of ideological subversion. It is a long interview with G. Edward Griffin.
why_hn: Cited in propaganda and disinformation threads, though some commenters present it more as a prediction of current events than established analysis.

title: ADL's Never Is Now 2019 | ADL International Leadership Award Presented to Sacha Baron Cohen
summary: Sacha Baron Cohen's speech accepting the ADL International Leadership Award, in which he criticizes social media companies for amplifying hate and propaganda. He argues that freedom of speech is not freedom of reach.
why_hn: Quoted heavily in moderation and free speech debates, particularly the line about freedom of speech and reach.

title: "You Have the Right to Remain Innocent" (James Duane)
summary: Law professor James Duane explains why you should not talk to the police even if you are innocent, drawing on case histories of wrongful convictions. It is a short version of the argument in his book on the right to remain silent.
why_hn: HN commenters send it to anyone who thinks innocent people have nothing to fear from answering police questions.

title: I Watched Ancient Apocalypse So You Don't Have To (Part 1)
summary: Miniminuteman begins a long, humorous point-by-point debunking of Graham Hancock's Netflix series Ancient Apocalypse and its claims of a lost ice-age civilization. It is part one of a multi-part critique.
why_hn: HN points people to it as an entertaining, thorough takedown of Hancock's pseudoarchaeology whenever his claims come up.

title: Cities: Skylines | Power, Politics, & Planning: Episode 1: Parking
summary: The first episode of a Cities: Skylines series on urban politics and planning, focused on parking. It uses the game to show how parking minimums shape cities, drawing on Donald Shoup's book The High Cost of Free Parking.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a clear illustration of how parking requirements produce car-centered, unwalkable American urban design.

title: Richard Feynman. Why.
summary: A short clip of Richard Feynman answering an interviewer's question about why magnets repel, explaining that a 'why' question depends on a shared framework of understanding. It illustrates how hard it is to explain fundamentals to a layperson.
why_hn: Cited constantly as the classic answer to 'why' questions, on explanation, frames of reference and the limits of physics.

title: Man Spends 30 Years Turning Degraded Land into Massive Forest – Fools & Dreamers (Full Documentary)
summary: Fools & Dreamers is a 30-minute documentary about Hinewai Nature Reserve in New Zealand, where botanist Hugh Wilson let gorse grow as a nurse canopy to regenerate native forest. It shows the results after 30 years and the local skepticism he faced.
why_hn: Shared in climate and land-use threads as a vivid example of how letting land regrow can restore forest.

title: Are Electric Cars Worse For The Environment? Myth Busted
summary: Engineering Explained works through whether electric cars are really worse for the environment than gasoline cars. It covers battery production emissions, the electricity mix used to charge, and how long an EV takes to break even on lifetime emissions.
why_hn: HN commenters link it repeatedly as a clear, number-based rebuttal to the claim that EVs are worse for the climate than gas cars.

title: How does Computer Memory Work? 💻🛠
summary: A 36-minute animated deep dive from Branch Education into how DRAM works. It shows how memory connects to the CPU and how billions of bits are stored in nanoscale capacitor cells. It also covers why DRAM sits between SSDs and the processor.
why_hn: Commenters recommend it as a clear, well-animated explanation of memory, especially for visual learners.

title: The Unanswered Question 1973 1  Musical Phonology Bernstein Norton
summary: Leonard Bernstein's 1973 Norton Lectures at Harvard, starting with Musical Phonology. He draws analogies between music and linguistics, including references to Chomsky.
why_hn: HN recommends it for a deep theory of why music sounds the way it does.

title: Raymond Hettinger, Keynote on Concurrency, PyBay 2017
summary: Raymond Hettinger's PyBay 2017 keynote on concurrency in Python. It covers threads, processes, asyncio, locks and the GIL, with live shell-based examples.
why_hn: Recommended as a clear, charismatic starting point for understanding Python concurrency and the GIL.

title: Marcus Aurelius' Meditations: The Stoic Ideal
summary: Michael Sugrue's lecture on Marcus Aurelius' Meditations and the Stoic ideal, covering the text and its philosophy. It is one of his humanities lectures known for their clarity.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a classic, clear introduction to Aurelius, with some saying it helped through hard times.

title: Don't Be the Last Person to Die
summary: CGP Grey argues that aging and death are a problem worth defeating, using a short animated essay. It is part of a pair with a follow-up from Kurzgesagt.
why_hn: HN longevity fans point to it as a concise, fun statement of the case for fighting aging, and some say it changed their minds.

title: Feynman: How to think 1 of 2  FUN TO IMAGINE 11
summary: An excerpt from the 1983 BBC series Fun to Imagine in which Richard Feynman describes how he and a mathematician friend counted in their heads in different ways, one verbally and one visually. It shows that people can reach the same goal through quite different mental methods.
why_hn: HN points to it constantly in threads on inner monologue, visual versus verbal thinking and communication as the classic, entertaining demonstration that minds work differently.

title: Joe Rogan Experience #606 - Randall Carlson
summary: A three-hour Joe Rogan podcast with Randall Carlson, builder and geomythologist, on catastrophic geological events, cosmic impacts and climate at the end of the last glacial period.
why_hn: Commenters in climate and impact-event threads send people to Carlson's Rogan appearances for his account of ancient cataclysms.

title: John Cleese vs Extremism
summary: A two-minute John Cleese monologue showing the pathology of extremism, explaining why it feels good and how it drives out moderates.
why_hn: Shared in heated-discussion threads as a short, witty take on why extremism is appealing.

title: Greg Young - CQRS and Event Sourcing - Code on the Beach 2014
summary: Greg Young's Code on the Beach 2014 talk on CQRS and event sourcing. He argues mature domains are built on facts that occurred rather than current state, and covers the business and technical benefits.
why_hn: HN developers recommend it as the talk that changed how they model systems, and as a clear intro to event sourcing's motivations.

title: 7 Minutes of Terror: The Challenges of Getting to Mars
summary: NASA JPL engineers explain the final minutes of the Curiosity rover's entry, descent and landing on Mars, which combined aerobraking, a parachute and a skycrane. It lays out the tight sequence of events that all had to work automatically.
why_hn: HN repeatedly recommends it as an awe-inspiring example of engineering problem solving and the go-to explainer on how Mars landings work.

title: Why Not Just: Think of AGI Like a Corporation?
summary: Robert Miles asks whether corporations can be thought of as artificial general superintelligences and how far the analogy holds. He argues the differences, such as being limited by employees' capabilities, matter for AI safety.
why_hn: HN points to it as an accessible rebuttal to the claim that AI risk is just corporate risk.

title: Stuart Halloway - Narcissistic Design
summary: Stuart Halloway's satirical talk describes how to protect yourself from industry change by spreading complexity through systems while following idiomatic practice. It uses this inversion to catalog software design anti-patterns.
why_hn: HN commenters love it as a witty and insightful tour of design anti-patterns, applicable to DSLs, OOP and API design.

title: Electron transport chain
summary: A short Harvard Online animated lesson on how the mitochondrial electron transport chain works. It shows proton pumping and the machinery that drives ATP synthesis.
why_hn: HN commenters share it to show how cells work as nanoscale machines, which many find mind-blowing.

title: The Map of Mathematics
summary: An animated 11-minute tour of the whole field of mathematics as a single map, showing how pure and applied math and their sub-fields relate to each other.
why_hn: Recommended to people asking how to self-learn math as a quick bird's-eye overview of the field.

title: This Is Water by David Foster Wallace Full Speech
summary: David Foster Wallace's 2005 commencement speech at Kenyon College, about the default settings of the mind, choosing what to pay attention to, and what we end up worshipping.
why_hn: HN people point lost, lonely or burned-out readers to it as a short, humane piece of perspective on how to live.

title: Civilizations at the End of Time: Iron Stars
summary: An Isaac Arthur episode on civilizations in the far future, past the Black Hole Era. It covers iron stars, Boltzmann brains, reversible computing and the idea of reversing entropy.
why_hn: HN recommends Isaac Arthur as an entry point for far-future and thermodynamic-endgame questions.

title: 4.5 Billion Years in 1 Hour
summary: Kurzgesagt's hour-long animated film that compresses Earth's 4.5 billion year history into one hour, roughly a million years per second. It follows the evolution of life through to humanity's tiny final stretch.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it for the sense of perspective it gives on deep time and how brief human history is.

title: The Bell Curve
summary: Shaun's roughly 2.7-hour video essay on The Bell Curve. It covers intelligence, the g factor, IQ tests, IQ versus environment and the politics behind the book, with a critical reading of the sources.
why_hn: HN commenters most often cite it as a thorough, well-sourced debunking of The Bell Curve and of popular IQ claims.

title: Immediate-Mode Graphical User Interfaces - 2005
summary: Casey Muratori's 2005 video introducing immediate-mode GUIs as an alternative to retained widget toolkits. He explains the motivation and shows minimal-state button logic.
why_hn: Seen as the origin of the IMGUI idea that inspired Dear ImGui, recommended to anyone curious about immediate-mode UI design.

title: Revolutionary Paint: How to Make Surfaces Stay Cool in the Sun
summary: Tech Ingredients shows how to make a homemade radiative cooling paint, with a custom liquid panel that cools below ambient temperature outdoors. The video covers the materials and how to apply the paint.
why_hn: HN points to it as an impressive, hands-on DIY demonstration of passive radiative cooling that works in practice.

title: Crash Course - The SMIDSY
summary: A motorcycle safety video on the SMIDSY (sorry mate, I didn't see you) accident, explaining the perception and optical illusion that makes drivers fail to see riders, and how riders can spot the signs and avoid it.
why_hn: HN considers it an outstanding explanation of why drivers miss motorcycles and cyclists, linked in threads on visibility and junction crashes.

title: BOLTR: DYSON HAIR DRYER. Is it WORTH the MONEY?
summary: AvE tears down a roughly $500 Dyson hair dryer, examining how its motor, airflow and electronics fit into a small body. He runs tests along the way and ultimately decides whether the engineering justifies the price.
why_hn: HN points to it as a favorite teardown, usually when discussing Dyson or how products are engineered and built, with some noting the host was impressed by the engineering.

title: How To Be Alone
summary: An animated short film of Tanya Davis's spoken-word poem 'How To Be Alone', illustrated by Andrea Dorfman. It gently argues that being alone can be embraced and enjoyed.
why_hn: HN commenters point lonely people to it as a moving, comforting piece of art about getting comfortable with solitude.

title: [AUDIO FIXED] The Truth Cannot be Sexist - Steven Pinker on the biology of sex differences
summary: An excerpt of the 2005 Harvard debate in which Steven Pinker gives his prepared case on biological sex differences and the under-representation of women in science. It covers cross-cultural patterns in preferences and abilities and the overlap between male and female distributions.
why_hn: Pointed to repeatedly in gender-in-tech threads, especially around the Google memo, as a science-based treatment of sex differences.

title: I Misunderstood the Greenhouse Effect. Here's How It Works.
summary: Sabine Hossenfelder explains how the greenhouse effect actually works, given that infrared is mostly absorbed low in the atmosphere already. She walks through why more CO2 still warms the surface.
why_hn: Recommended as an accessible, nuanced explanation of the mechanics of global warming, including the saturation puzzle.

title: a better way to count
summary: jan Misali presents an humorous but earnest case for counting in base 6 (seximal) instead of base 10 or 12, comparing the arithmetic advantages of each.
why_hn: HN points to it as a funny, convincing take on number bases whenever dozenal or base 6 comes up.

title: But what is a Fourier series?  From heat flow to drawing with circles | DE4
summary: 3Blue1Brown introduces Fourier series, from the heat equation to drawing arbitrary shapes with rotating circles. It builds a visual intuition for decomposing functions into sine waves.
why_hn: Recommended as the visual explanation that makes Fourier series and transforms click, even for laypeople.

title: Learn music theory in half an hour.
summary: Andrew Huang teaches the basics of music theory in about half an hour, covering intervals, chords and patterns. He stresses understanding how music works over memorizing terminology.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a concise, approachable starting point for anyone asking how to learn music theory.

title: Real Analysis, Lecture 1: Constructing the Rational Numbers
summary: The first lecture of Francis Su's Harvey Mudd real analysis course, covering the construction of the rational numbers. It begins a full lecture series that follows a standard analysis text.
why_hn: HN people recommend Su's lectures for building real analysis intuition, citing his phenomenal teaching style.

title: How Prince of Persia Defeated Apple II's Memory Limitations | War Stories | Ars Technica
summary: In an Ars Technica War Stories episode, Prince of Persia creator Jordan Mechner describes how he made the game on the Apple II, fighting hardware memory limits and the platform's decline. It covers the rotoscoped animation and the engineering tricks involved.
why_hn: Repeatedly called essential viewing for game development history and clever work under memory constraints.

title: Operation InfeKtion: How Russia Perfected the Art of War | NYT Opinion
summary: A New York Times Opinion documentary tracing Soviet and KGB disinformation, from the 1980s AIDS origin hoax to modern campaigns like Pizzagate. It features former KGB officers and the people who tried to counter the lies.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as a clear explanation of how disinformation campaigns work and where today's tactics came from.

title: Tearing Down the Model T of Our Time - Autoline After Hours 284
summary: An Autoline After Hours episode where Sandy Munro discusses his complete teardown of the BMW i3, along with automotive journalists. It covers the car's carbon fiber construction and manufacturing technology.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a fascinating look at the i3's revolutionary materials and production methods, and as a contrast point for Tesla.

title: How one tweet can ruin your life | Jon Ronson
summary: Jon Ronson's TED talk on public shaming on Twitter, centered on Justine Sacco and others whose lives were upended by online mobs. He argues we have become a baying crowd and should rethink how we treat each other online.
why_hn: HN commenters bring it up in threads about online mobs and cancellation as a relevant talk by a journalist who interviewed shamed people.

title: End of Space – Creating a Prison for Humanity
summary: Kurzgesagt explains how accumulating space junk could trigger a collision cascade (Kessler syndrome) that makes launches too dangerous and traps humanity on Earth.
why_hn: The standard explainer HN links in satellite and debris threads for the collision-cascade risk.

title: It's Not About The Nail
summary: A two-minute comedy sketch in which a woman describes her problems while a visible nail sticks out of her head, and her partner keeps trying to fix it instead of listening. It dramatizes the gap between wanting empathy and being offered solutions.
why_hn: HN commenters link it as the quickest memorable illustration of listening versus problem-solving, and as shorthand in threads on empathy and support.

title: Animated Voting Methods
summary: An animated simulation comparing single-winner voting methods such as plurality, instant runoff and STAR. Colored regions show which candidate wins as a randomized electorate shifts across a two-dimensional political space, building on Ka-Ping Yee's earlier diagrams.
why_hn: HN commenters cite it in voting-reform threads as a visual argument that cardinal systems (STAR, approval) beat plurality and ranked-choice voting.

title: Dr. Satchin Panda on Time-Restricted Feeding and Its Effects on Obesity, Muscle Mass & Heart Health
summary: Rhonda Patrick interviews Salk Institute researcher Satchidananda Panda about circadian rhythms and the timing of food. They cover time-restricted feeding and its links to obesity, muscle mass, heart health, and light exposure.
why_hn: Recommended in threads on fasting and nutrition as a deep dive from the lead researcher on time-restricted eating.

title: Velocity 2012:  Richard Cook, "How Complex Systems Fail"
summary: Dr. Richard Cook, a physician and patient safety researcher, presents his ideas on how complex systems fail, at Velocity 2012. He argues for designing for resiliency rather than trying to exhaustively handle every failure mode.
why_hn: HN people recommend it as a must-watch for anyone running complex systems, and some rewatch it regularly to remember its principles.

title: Flat Earth: A Measured Response
summary: hbomberguy investigates the modern flat earth movement and why people come to believe it. The video treats the community with a measured, humorous tone and looks at the social causes behind the belief.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as an entertaining and thoughtful look at flat earthers that frames the belief as a distrust of failing institutions.

title: RSA ANIMATE: Language as a Window into Human Nature
summary: An RSA Animate in which Steven Pinker explains how the mind builds infinite meanings from finite language, and why people often speak indirectly. It covers ambiguity, politeness and mutual knowledge, including the emperor's new clothes example.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a short, clear explanation of why people avoid saying things explicitly and how common knowledge works socially and politically.

title: Noam Chomsky: The five filters of the mass media machine | The Listening Post
summary: A short Al Jazeera animation narrated by Amy Goodman presenting Noam Chomsky's five filters of the mass media: ownership, advertising, media elite sourcing, flak and a common enemy. It is part of the MediaTheorised series.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a quick, accessible introduction to the propaganda model from Manufacturing Consent.

title: Pop an ollie and innovate! | Rodney Mullen | TED
summary: Skateboarding pioneer Rodney Mullen talks about how the open skate community and its environments drive the invention of new tricks out of pure passion. He draws parallels to collaboration and open source.
why_hn: HN people share it as an inspiring talk linking skateboarding creativity to hacking and open-source knowledge sharing.

title: Jordan Walke - React to the Future
summary: Jordan Walke, creator of React, talks at ReasonConf 2019 about the ideas behind ReasonML and how it extends React's programming model with OCaml. He also discusses why familiar syntax matters.
why_hn: HN recommends it as the best introduction to Reason's motivations, straight from React's creator.

title: How I overcame alcoholism | Claudia Christian | TEDxLondonBusinessSchool
summary: Actress Claudia Christian tells how she overcame alcoholism using the Sinclair Method, which uses naltrexone to gradually reduce cravings. She discusses fresh perspectives on treating alcohol use disorder.
why_hn: HN commenters share it as the talk that introduced them to the Sinclair Method as an alternative approach to alcohol dependence.

title: DropBox Demo
summary: The original five-minute Dropbox demo video, which presented the product's features before a finished product existed. It was aimed at technical early adopters and became famous as a launch strategy.
why_hn: HN cites it as the classic example of validating a product idea with a demo video, and many recall how compelling it was.

title: Slaughterbots
summary: Slaughterbots is a fictional short film, backed by Stuart Russell, depicting swarms of cheap autonomous drones that use facial recognition to assassinate targets. It was made to argue for banning autonomous weapons.
why_hn: HN invokes it as the standard reference whenever drone swarms, autonomous weapons or military AI come up in the news.

title: Hamming, Intro to The Art of Doing Science and Engineering: Learning to Learn (March 28, 1995)
primary_topic: learning to learn and doing science
summary: The introductory lecture of Richard Hamming's capstone course, The Art of Doing Science and Engineering: Learning to Learn. It focuses on style of thinking and on educating rather than training, using technical material only as illustration.

title: The world depends on a collection of strange items. They're not cheap
summary: Veritasium visits NIST to explain Standard Reference Materials, the carefully characterized items such as peanut butter used to calibrate instruments and keep measurements consistent. It covers why they exist and why they are expensive.
why_hn: Whenever NIST's pricey peanut butter or reference materials come up, commenters point to this as the clear explanation of why they exist.

title: Lecture: Biblical Series I: Introduction to the Idea of God
summary: Jordan Peterson's first lecture in his Biblical Series examines the idea of God as sovereignty and power abstracted from any individual ruler, and as the pattern inherent in human dominance hierarchies.
why_hn: HN fans say it offers value even to atheists by interpreting Bible stories as psychological and evolutionary archetypes, and some credit it with helping them through depression.

title: Gabriella Gonzalez – How to market Haskell to a mainstream programmer
summary: Gabriella Gonzalez argues that developers misunderstand marketing as deception or hype, and applies the technology-adoption ideas of Crossing the Chasm to Haskell. She looks at what keeps Haskell from reaching mainstream programmers and what a community can do about it.
why_hn: Commenters point to it as a clear take on why functional languages stall outside niches, and its lessons are seen as applying to any technology trying to go mainstream.

title: Should We Colonize Venus Instead of Mars?
summary: A PBS Space Time episode asking whether Venus would be a better colonization target than Mars. It covers Venus's habitable altitudes, floating balloon habitats, and the term surfacism.
why_hn: HN links it in Mars-colonization threads as a concise case for Venus.

title: The surprising pattern behind color names around the world
summary: Vox explains the Berlin and Kay research showing that languages around the world tend to invent color words in the same order. It walks through the hierarchy and the debate around it.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as a clear, well-made summary of the linguistics of color naming and how culture shapes it.

title: 7 Minutes of Terror: Curiosity Rover's Risky Mars Landing | Video
summary: NASA's animated explanation of the Curiosity rover's Mars landing, which relied on a complex automated sequence taking about seven minutes. It features NASA engineers discussing the risks before the 2012 landing.
why_hn: Recommended as a gripping look at how hard Mars entry, descent and landing is.

title: This giant model stopped a terrible plan
summary: Tom Scott tells how John Reber's plan to dam San Francisco Bay was disproved by the Army Corps of Engineers' giant hydraulic Bay Model in Sausalito. The model showed the plan would have been dangerously wrong.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a short, fascinating story of a scale model preventing a terrible engineering decision.

title: Why do competitors open their stores next to one another? - Jac de Haan
summary: A short animated TED-Ed lesson in which two competing ice cream vendors on a beach illustrate why rival shops cluster together. It introduces game theory and the Nash equilibrium through the Hotelling model.
why_hn: HN people use it as a clear, quick explanation of Nash equilibrium and why competitors cluster.

title: Tesla Battery Day
summary: Tesla's 2020 Battery Day event, with a company update and a keynote on new cell design, manufacturing, vertical integration and cheaper lithium and materials. It ends with the Plaid Model S and a Q&A.
why_hn: Treated as the essential primary source for Tesla's battery and cost-reduction plans, and a feast for engineering nerds.

title: Ubuntu Slaughters Kittens | BSD Now 103
summary: A BSD Now episode featuring a long interview with Joyent CTO Bryan Cantrill on dtrace, ZFS, pkgsrc, containers and more. It includes his rant on why Linux epoll is flawed and stories from Sun.
why_hn: HN links it for Cantrill's entertaining epoll versus kqueue rant and his stories, such as bricking a machine with rm -rf.

title: The Daily Show - Burn Noticed
summary: A Daily Show with Jon Stewart segment from 2014 covering the People's Climate March in New York and a House science committee struggling with basic global warming facts. It mixes satire with an argument against climate denial.
why_hn: Commenters call it a favorite Daily Show clip and link it as a ready answer to climate-skeptic arguments.

title: Louis CK Everything Is Amazing And Nobody Is Happy
summary: A clip of Louis CK on Conan riffing that everything is amazing and nobody is happy, about people complaining over airplane wifi and taking modern technology for granted.
why_hn: HN invokes it whenever people grumble about convenience, technology or AI that would have seemed miraculous not long ago.

title: I'm Allowed to Rob You!
summary: A short anarchist-leaning video by Larken Rose arguing that the Constitution and similar documents cannot legitimately grant anyone the right to take other people's property. It uses a rhetorical 'paper that lets me rob you' setup to challenge belief in political authority.
why_hn: Libertarian-minded commenters post it in surveillance, government and constitution threads as a red-pill argument that political authority is illusory.

title: Single particle creates interference after double slit - Wave particle duality at the workshop
summary: A short demo of a walking droplet on a vibrating silicone oil bath passing through a double slit and producing interference, a macro-scale analogue of pilot-wave behavior.
why_hn: HN users share it to build intuition about wave-particle duality and pilot-wave ideas in quantum mechanics threads.

title: How The Auto Industry Carjacked The American Dream | Climate Town
summary: A Climate Town video on how the auto industry reshaped American cities and culture through advertising, lobbying and campaigns like the 1939 World's Fair. It is snarky in tone but backed by a published source document.
why_hn: Recommended in urbanism threads as a well-sourced account of how car dependency was manufactured.

title: Don't Say Velcro
summary: Velcro Brand's legal team makes a short, humorous ad asking people not to use "velcro" as a noun or verb and to say hook and loop instead. It is a tongue-in-cheek lesson in defending a trademark against genericization.
why_hn: HN cites it as the go-to example of a company defending its trademark, and many also find it funny.

title: Telescope Building with John Dobson
summary: A roughly 90-minute film of John Dobson building a Dobsonian telescope step by step, including hand-grinding the mirror.
why_hn: Recommended to anyone interested in telescope making as a guide from Dobson himself.

title: Randomness is Random - Numberphile
summary: Numberphile with Simon Pampena on how humans misunderstand randomness, including coin-flip sequences, run lengths and the gambler's fallacy.
why_hn: Recommended as an accessible demonstration that people are bad at producing or judging random sequences.

title: Building a Marsbase is a Horrible Idea: Let’s do it!
summary: A Kurzgesagt animation walking through how a Mars base could be built and why it would be punishing, covering radiation, temperature extremes, toxic dust and the need for shielding.
why_hn: Recommended as a sobering, accessible overview of the practical challenges of living on Mars.

title: The Dark Side of Counter-Strike 2
summary: Coffeezilla's investigation into the Counter-Strike 2 skin gambling ecosystem, covering casino sites, influencers and esports teams that profit from it. It is part of a multi-part series on Valve's skin economy and its effects on young players.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as an investigative look at CS skin gambling and the exploitation of minors.

title: Don't Be a Sucker
summary: A 1945 US Army educational film that dramatizes how demagogues use prejudice and scapegoating to divide people. It opens with fake wrestling matches and crooked gambling games to show how con artists work, then applies the lesson to racial and religious bigotry.
why_hn: HN commenters bring it up in political threads as a classic warning about divisive agitators and fascism, and suggest it be remade for each generation.

title: Your Brain: Who's in Control? | Full Documentary | NOVA | PBS
summary: A NOVA documentary with neuroscientist Heather Berlin exploring the subconscious and what drives our decisions. It uses sleepwalking, anesthesia, improvised rap in an MRI and game theory to probe how much of the brain's work is hidden.
why_hn: Recommended in threads on consciousness, anesthesia and perception as a fascinating look at how much of experience the brain constructs.

title: KEYNOTE / Robert Erdmann
summary: Robert Erdmann, a materials scientist at the Rijksmuseum, gives a PyCon keynote on the ultra-high-resolution imaging of Rembrandt's Night Watch. He covers the automated gantry camera system, the Python software that drives it, and the large volumes of image data involved.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as a technically jaw-dropping talk, and it is the standard reference whenever the Night Watch gigapixel images come up.

title: Steve Jobs on Failure
primary_topic: fear of failure and asking for help
summary: A two-minute clip from a 1994 interview with Steve Jobs by the Santa Clara Valley Historical Association. Jobs talks about failure and about how most people never ask for help, recalling that he simply called people to ask.
why_hn: HN commenters return to it as a motivational reminder to not fear failure and to just ask for what you want.

title: Desert Storm - The Air War, Day 1 - Animated
summary: An animated account of Day 1 of the Desert Storm air war on 17 January 1991, covering the 2,775 sorties flown against Iraqi strategic targets in the first 24 hours.
why_hn: Recommended as a deeply researched, visual series that shows how overwhelming the coalition air campaign was.

title: Astroturf and manipulation of media messages | Sharyl Attkisson | TEDxUniversityofNevada
summary: Investigative journalist Sharyl Attkisson explains how astroturf, fake grassroots campaigns funded by corporate or political interests, manipulates media messages. The TEDx talk is about 11 minutes.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as an introduction to shills, astroturfing and lobbyist influence on media, especially in threads about fake news and online forums.

title: How to Enhance Your Gut Microbiome for Brain & Overall Health
summary: A Huberman Lab podcast episode on the gut-brain axis and how the gut microbiome affects the nervous system, hunger and overall health. It covers the pathways by which the gut influences the brain and practical steps for gut health.
why_hn: Recommended as an accessible neuroscientist's overview of gut microbiome science with practical takeaways.

title: Angry Voicemail We Got From an Alamo Drafthouse Customer
summary: Alamo Drafthouse posted an angry voicemail from a customer who was kicked out for texting in the theater. The theater turned it into a humorous in-house preview.
why_hn: It is cited as a viral example of Alamo enforcing its no-talking and no-texting rules with humor.

title: Crow skiing down a roof
summary: A one-minute clip of a crow repeatedly sliding down a snowy roof on a small lid, apparently just for fun.
why_hn: Offered as vivid evidence that animals, crows in particular, play for pleasure and display intelligence beyond survival needs.

title: How We’re Fooled By Statistics
summary: A short Veritasium video explaining regression to the mean and how ignoring it leads to wrong conclusions about punishment versus reward, medical treatments and sports streaks. It uses the example of flight instructors who believed criticism works better than praise.
why_hn: HN commenters link it as the clearest short explanation of regression to the mean, especially for how it misleads people about feedback and statistics.

title: "The Dangerous Truth About Protein" - Janice Stanger, Ph.D.
summary: A presentation by Janice Stanger arguing that protein is overhyped and that excess or the wrong kinds of protein are harmful. It promotes a whole-foods, plant-based diet.
why_hn: A few commenters cite it as a starting point for the claim that excess protein is harmful, though the claims are one-sided advocacy.

title: Michael Bay - What is Bayhem?
summary: An Every Frame a Painting video essay on Michael Bay's style, 'Bayhem', covering his camera movement, composition, color and editing. It argues that even if you dislike his films, they teach something about visual perception.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a short, well-produced and eye-opening piece of film analysis.

title: Money as Debt I - Revised Edition 2009 (Full Movie)
summary: An animated documentary by Paul Grignon explaining how modern money is created through bank lending as debt. This is a combined upload of the revised 2009 edition.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as a cartoonish but thorough explanation of the monetary system, though some critics dispute its claims.

title: Music as a Language: Victor Wooten at TEDxGabriolaIsland
summary: Bassist Victor Wooten argues that music should be learned the way children learn their first language: by immersion and play, without early correction or rigid academic instruction. He draws on how babies pick up speech from the people around them.
why_hn: HN commenters point to it when discussing how to teach children or beginners, as a language-like alternative to formal instruction.

title: MEETING THE ENEMY A feminist comes to terms with the Men's Rights movement | Cassie Jaye | TEDxMarin
summary: Documentary filmmaker Cassie Jaye explains how making The Red Pill led her, a feminist, to reevaluate her assumptions about the Men's Rights movement. She argues for listening to people you think of as the enemy.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a thoughtful account from a feminist on men's issues and the cost of saying unpopular things.

title: Stephen Wolfram: Complexity and the Fabric of Reality | Lex Fridman Podcast #234
summary: A long Lex Fridman interview with Stephen Wolfram on complexity, cellular automata, computational irreducibility and the Wolfram Physics Project.
why_hn: HN recommends it as an accessible way into Wolfram's physics ideas and his personality.

title: Money as Debt - Full Documentary
summary: Paul Grignon's animated documentary presenting his view of how banks create money as debt and why that system requires continuous growth. It outlines the historical background of modern banking.
why_hn: Recommended as an approachable explanation of fractional reserve banking, with the caveat that it is biased.

title: Stephan T. Lavavej “Floating-Point ＜charconv＞: Making Your Code 10x Faster With C++17's Final Boss”
hn_categories: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages
summary: Stephan T. Lavavej's CppCon 2019 talk on implementing floating-point to_chars and from_chars in Microsoft's C++ STL. It covers the history of float-string conversion and the algorithms that make it much faster.
why_hn: HN calls it a surprisingly fun, approachable talk on a hard problem and cites it in floating-point threads.

title: Procedurally Crafting Manhattan for Marvel's Spider-Man
summary: GDC 2019 session where Insomniac's David Santiago describes the procedural systems used to build Manhattan for Marvel's Spider-Man. It covers the open-world pipeline and how each system was designed to support iteration and dependencies.
why_hn: Recommended as a prime example of large-scale procedural generation used in a shipped AAA game.

title: Email Hates the Living
summary: A lightning-style conference talk by Ricardo Signes about the horrors of email: its protocols, formats and decades of accumulated quirks. It is delivered with a humorous horror theme to show why handling email correctly is harder than it looks.
why_hn: HN points to it whenever someone underestimates how hard email parsing, validation or building a mail client really is.

title: 1. Climate Change -- the scientific debate
summary: The first video in potholer54's climate series, giving a basic look at how climate scientists infer that man-made carbon gases are changing the climate. It is a short explainer meant to present the scientific evidence plainly.
why_hn: HN users point to it as a clear, evidence-based series to counter climate skepticism.

title: Sample Breakdown: Daft Punk - One More Time
summary: A short Tracklib video visualizing the disco sample that Daft Punk's One More Time is built from. It shows how the track is composed from the original material.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a striking visual breakdown of how the song was constructed.

title: Yuri Bezmenov: Psychological Warfare Subversion & Control of Western Society (Complete)
summary: A 1983 Los Angeles lecture by KGB defector Yuri Bezmenov on how the Soviets carried out ideological subversion of target societies through propaganda. He walks through demoralization and normalization stages.
why_hn: HN commenters link it to argue that cultural subversion and normalization are playing out today, though mostly as a reference in unrelated threads.

title: Joe Rogan Experience #1080 - David Goggins
summary: Joe Rogan interviews David Goggins, a retired Navy SEAL and ultramarathon runner, about his path from overweight to elite endurance athlete and pushing beyond comfort zones.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as an inspiring story about perseverance and getting outside one's comfort zone.

title: The Kennedy Assassination: Inside the Book Depository
summary: A 98-minute LEMMiNO video reconstructing what happened inside the Texas School Book Depository before, during, and after the Kennedy assassination. It draws on testimony to map people's movements and discrepancies.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a detailed, well-sourced overview that helps viewers form their own opinion.

title: What P vs NP is actually about
summary: Polylog explains how algorithms can be turned into circuits and encoded as satisfiability problems, which lets you effectively run them backwards. It uses this to motivate breaking RSA, general reductions to SAT, and what P vs NP is really asking.
why_hn: Recommended as an intuitive, animated explanation of P vs NP framed around reversing computation.

title: Making of "The Prodigy - Voodoo People" in Ableton by Jim Pavloff
summary: Jim Pavloff rebuilds The Prodigy's 'Voodoo People' in Ableton from its listed samples. The video shows how the track is assembled and how close a handmade reconstruction can sound.
why_hn: Used as an example of prototyping music and, in a Copilot copyright thread, of a handmade reconstruction that sounds like the original.

title: Robust-first computing: Beyond efficiency
summary: Dave Ackley gives a high-level introduction to robust-first computing, which prioritizes robustness over efficiency in computer architecture. A sorting demo illustrates the idea.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a short, clear explanation of robust-first computing by its originator, and as a philosophy relevant to building with unreliable components like LLMs.

title: Vaccines and Autism: A Measured Response
summary: hbomberguy's long video dissects the anti-vaccine movement, analyzing Andrew Wakefield's fraudulent MMR-autism study, the media's role and Wakefield's loss of his license. It combines detailed research with humor.
why_hn: HN commenters call it the definitive, thorough answer to whether vaccines cause autism and recommend it as an entertaining deep dive.

title: I BOUGHT A WHOLE CHURCH ORGAN - Part 1 The Organs Removal
summary: Part one of Look Mum No Computer's series on buying a whole church pipe organ, covering how it was removed from its home. The series goes on to restoring it and rewiring it for MIDI.
why_hn: HN recommends the series as great fun, following a talented and enthusiastic amateur rebuilding a pipe organ.

title: Derren Brown - The System (Full)
summary: Derren Brown's TV special in which he convinces a person he has a system for predicting horse race winners, demonstrating how survivorship bias and selective outcomes can fake predictive powers.
why_hn: HN cites it as the classic demonstration of survivorship and confirmation bias in betting, trading and prediction claims.

title: Terence Mckenna - Culture is your operating system
summary: A short edited excerpt of Terence McKenna arguing that culture acts as an operating system for the mind, set to imagery and music. It touches on psychedelics and how they change thinking.
why_hn: Cited as the origin of the 'culture/philosophy as operating system' metaphor and as a quick introduction to McKenna's ideas.
